extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy, logic, and the foundations of science
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-level philosophical analysis of the nature, origin, and evidential status of axioms, definitions, arithmetic, algebra, and deductive (demonstrative) sciences; argues that these are ultimately inductive/hypothetical and examines limits of mathematical certainty. Useful for understanding how to assess claims of necessity and self-evidence in science and mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axioms as inductions from experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Axioms of demonstrative sciences are inductions from experience — the simplest and most universal generalizations from facts rather than truths known a priori.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text asserts that axioms rest on 'superabundant and obvious evidence' and that the burden of proof lies on those who claim any other origin for them. Treat axioms as experimentally grounded generalizations: they are certain only if the underlying empirical generalization holds. (Original phrasing: 'we have thought ourselves warranted in concluding that axioms are but a class, the most universal class, of inductions from experience; the simplest and easiest cases of generalization from the facts furnished to us by our senses or by our internal consciousness.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions as generalized fictions (not exact truths)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions in deductive sciences function as convenient generalizations from experience that often deny modifying properties; the denial is a deliberate fiction to exclude complicating circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions assert of some kind of object some properties observed to belong to it while denying other accompanying properties to simplify reasoning; this exclusion is a useful supposition when modifiers are trivial or can be postponed. (Original idea: definitions 'are not even, accurately speaking, truths; being propositions in which... we at the same time deny that it possesses any other properties, though in truth other properties do in every individual instance accompany... The denial, therefore, is a mere fiction.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive (demonstrative) sciences are hypothetical
rubrics_metrics.description: Deductive sciences proceed by tracing consequences of assumptions; their conclusions are true conditional on suppositions which are approximations to truth, so the sciences are hypothetical in method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One must separate (a) deducing what follows from given assumptions (demonstrative science) from (b) deciding whether those assumptions are actually true (an empirical inquiry). The 'peculiar certainty' of deduction arises from certainty of inference under the supposition, not from unconditional empirical truth of premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetic and algebra are not merely verbal substitutions
rubrics_metrics.description: The view that number-theory and algebra are only transformations of language (nominalism) is mistaken; arithmetic and algebra include genuine inductions and concern 'things', not just signs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although algebraic symbols often do not evoke concrete images, their manipulations carry probative force because they stand for magnitudes or numbers applicable to all things; the inferences are about things in general rather than mere synonyms. The text explains how symbols like a, b, x represent 'all things whatever' and why algebraic reasoning is not purely verbal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical truths rest on sensory/empirical evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Fundamental arithmetical propositions (e.g., 'two and one is three') are grounded in sensory demonstrations—showing collections of objects and their re-arrangements to the senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaching arithmetic via objects (pebbles, balls) exemplifies the empirical basis: the propositions are inductive truths learned by observation and manipulation. The chapter emphasizes that these are physical facts about separable collections that the senses verify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical certainty limited to pure number
rubrics_metrics.description: What is commonly called mathematical certainty (unconditional truth and perfect accuracy) strictly applies only to pure number (number-as-number), not to quantity when units or other attributes enter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arithmetic is applied to real-world quantities, hidden hypotheses (e.g., equality of units) are introduced; thus certainty becomes conditional. Examples: one pound + one pound presumes equivalent pounds (troy vs avoirdupois); horse-power assumes horses of equal strength. For pure counts (population size), arithmetic conclusions hold without such hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for equality of units condition in arithmetic
rubrics_metrics.description: Arithmetic implicitly assumes that the units being counted are equal in the relevant respects (1=1); if this condition is doubtful, arithmetical propositions may fail to hold in intended meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the hypothetical element even in number: when inferring equality or inequality of other properties from counts, one must assume unit-equivalence. The chapter gives statistical examples where mere counting is sufficient, but warns that inferring other properties requires verifying the unit-equality assumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrative science as preparation of inferences from assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrative (deductive) science is the enterprise of working out once-for-all the consequences of given assumptions so that when particular cases arise one can apply the pre-determined inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method economizes effort: do the logical/deductive work in advance (what follows if assumptions were true), and leave empirical work (are assumptions sufficiently true here?) to be settled case-by-case by observation or further argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimate use of reductio ad absurdum to test assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reductio ad absurdum is a valid method to demonstrate the falsity of an assumption by showing it leads to contradiction or to conclusions incompatible with known facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deduction can legitimately proceed from fictitious or false assumptions for the purpose of exposing their falsity; historical examples include Ptolemy and Descartes using false assumptions to build systems, and reductio is explicitly used to show incompatible consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratiocination is not ultimately founded on reductio ad absurdum
rubrics_metrics.description: Although many logical demonstrations use reductio, the ground of ratiocination is not reducible to reductio alone; rather it rests on the basic maxim that 'whatever has a mark has what it is a mark of'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter argues that forcing assent via a reductio presupposes ratiocination itself; one cannot ultimately compel assent by a second syllogism if the first is rejected. The fundamental maxim of inference (about marks and what they indicate) underlies correct argument rather than reductio being the final foundation.
